items.title: Joan of Arc was burned at Rouen in 1431, aged 19
items.claim: What did Joan of Arc achieve before her execution?

options.text: Nothing — her story is later legend

She convinced Charles VII she had divine guidance, led French forces to relieve the siege of Orléans in May 1429, helped recover Reims and have Charles crowned (July 1429); captured by Burgundians, sold to the English, tried for heresy and burned at Rouen on 30 May 1431
She was a Burgundian general who switched sides
She was canonised within months of her death

items.reveal:
Joan was a peasant from Domrémy who claimed visions of St Michael, St Catherine and St Margaret from age 13. After persuading Charles's court at Chinon, she joined the relief of Orléans aged 17. The siege was lifted in nine days; Reims (the traditional coronation city) was retaken; Charles VII was crowned on 17 July 1429.

She was captured at Compiègne (May 1430), held for ransom by the Burgundians, sold to the English, and tried by a French ecclesiastical court at Rouen. The trial of 1455-56 (after the English left) annulled the conviction. She was canonised in 1920.

The Hundred Years War ended in French victory at Castillon (1453).
items.why: The Hundred Years War's turning point is a teenager with no military training. Joan of Arc's trial transcripts survive — she remains one of the most documented medieval figures and a case in how religion, war and gender intersect.

items.title: McCarthy was censured by his own Senate in 1954
items.claim: How did Joseph McCarthy's anti-communist campaign end?

options.text: After televised Army-McCarthy hearings exposed his methods, the Senate voted 67-22 to censure him on 2 December 1954; he died of liver failure in 1957 aged 48
He resigned and joined the Republican Party leadership

items.reveal:
McCarthy had risen on a 1950 Wheeling speech claiming 205 communists in the State Department. The Army-McCarthy hearings (April-June 1954) were televised; Army counsel Joseph Welch's 'Have you no sense of decency, sir?' on 9 June became the iconic moment.

Edward R. Murrow's CBS broadcast 'See It Now' on 9 March 1954 had already turned mainstream opinion. The Senate censure vote followed in December.

HUAC (House Un-American Activities Committee), the Hollywood blacklist, loyalty oaths and the Smith Act prosecutions continued separately and outlasted McCarthy.
items.why: McCarthyism as a phenomenon was bigger than McCarthy. His fall did not end the Red Scare — but it ended one specific style of grandstanding accusation, and television was central to both his rise and fall.

items.title: Hastings lasted nearly a full day and was won by a feigned retreat
items.claim: The Battle of Hastings (14 October 1066) is often remembered as a swift Norman triumph. What actually happened?

options.text: William routed Harold's army within an hour
Fighting lasted from around 9 a.m. to dusk; the Anglo-Saxon shield-wall held until Norman cavalry used feigned retreats to draw housecarls down Senlac Hill, exposing the line
The English never engaged — they fled at the sight of Norman cavalry
The battle was decided by a single cavalry charge at dawn

items.reveal_title: A near thing on Senlac Hill
items.reveal:
William of Poitiers and the Bayeux Tapestry both record the day-long fight. Harold's army held the high ground in a shield-wall formation; William's archers, infantry and cavalry attacked uphill. A rumour that William had died spread early; he raised his helmet to show his face and rally his troops.

The feigned retreats — possibly accidental at first, then deliberate — broke the discipline of the shield-wall. Harold was killed late in the day along with his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine.

William was not crowned at Westminster until 25 December 1066. Anglo-Saxon resistance continued for years (the Harrying of the North, 1069-70).
items.why: 1066 looks decisive in retrospect. On the day it was a hill-defence that nearly held — and might have, if not for a tactical innovation. Contingency in military history.
